**Hydrogen – A Quick Reference to Its Key Properties**

| Category | Property | Value / Description |
|----------|----------|---------------------|
| **Basic Atomic Data** | Atomic number | 1 |
| | Atomic mass (average) | 1.008 u |
| | Electron configuration | 1s¹ |
| | Isotopes | H‑1 (protium), H‑2 (deuterium), H‑3 (tritium) |
| | Nuclear spin | ½ (protium), 0 (deuterium), ½ (tritium) |
| | Natural abundance | ~99.98 % protium, ~0.02 % deuterium, trace tritium |
| **Physical State (25 °C, 1 atm)** | State | Gas |
| | Color | Colorless |
| | Odor | Odorless |
| | Taste | Tasteless |
| | Density | 0.08988 g L⁻¹ (≈1/14 of air) |
| | Boiling point | –252.87 °C (−423.17 °F) |
| | Melting point | –259.16 °C (−434.49 °F) |
| | Vapor pressure | 1 atm at 20.28 °C |
| | Specific heat (gas) | 14.304 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (at constant pressure) |
| | Heat of vaporization | 0.452 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| | Speed of sound | ~1270 m s⁻¹ (in pure H₂) |
| | Refractive index | 1.000132 (at 589 nm) |
| **Chemical Properties** | Electronegativity (Pauling) | 2.20 |
| | Ionization energy | 13.598 eV (first) |
| | Electron affinity | –0.754 eV |
| | Oxidation states | +1 (most common), –1 (hydride) |
| | Bond dissociation energy (H–H) | 436 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| | Standard enthalpy of formation | 0 kJ mol⁻¹ (by definition for elemental H₂) |
| | Standard Gibbs free energy of formation | 0 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| | pKa of H₃⁺ (in water) | –7.0 (very strong acid) |
| | pKa of H₂O (as base) | 15.7 |
| | Flammability | Extremely flammable; explosive mixture with air (4–75 % H₂) |
| | Combustion reaction | 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O (ΔH ≈ –286 kJ mol⁻¹) |
| | Solubility in water | 1.6 g L⁻¹ at 25 °C (≈0.0006 mol L⁻¹) |
| | Solubility in organic solvents | Very low in most, but higher in supercritical CO₂ |
| **Isotopic Variants** | Protium (¹H) | Stable, most abundant |
| | Deuterium (²H) | Stable, 1 in 6000 atoms; heavier, lower zero‑point energy |
| | Tritium (³H) | Radioactive (β⁻ decay, t½ ≈ 12.32 y) |
| | Molecular forms | H₂, HD, D₂, HT, DT, T₂ |
| **Nuclear & Astrophysical** | Role in stars | Fusion of H into He powers stars; proton–proton chain, CNO cycle |
| | Solar abundance | ~74 % by mass |
| | Fusion reaction (pp‑chain) | 4 p → ⁴He + 2 e⁺ + 2 νₑ + γ |
| | Energy released per fusion | ~26.7 MeV |
| | Tritium half‑life | 12.32 years (β⁻ decay to ³He) |
| | Tritium in nuclear weapons | Used as a neutron source in boosted fission devices |
| **Applications & Uses** | Fuel cell technology | H₂ + O₂ → H₂O (electrochemical) |
| | Rocket propellant | Liquid H₂ + liquid O₂ (LH₂/LOX) |
| | Metallurgy | Reducing agent for iron ore, steelmaking |
| | Chemical synthesis | Hydride reagents (LiAlH₄, NaBH₄) |
| | Medical imaging | Deuterated compounds in NMR, PET tracers |
| | Energy storage | Hydrogen storage in metal hydrides, high‑pressure tanks, cryogenic liquefaction |
| **Safety & Handling** | Explosion limits | Lower: 4 %, Upper: 75 % (air) |
| | Ignition energy | 0.02 mJ (very low) |
| | Health hazards | Inhalation of high concentrations → hypoxia; tritium exposure → radiation risk |
| | Environmental impact | Greenhouse gas potential if released; but low global warming potential compared to CO₂ |

---

### Quick Takeaways

- **Hydrogen is the simplest and most abundant element** in the universe, existing mainly as a diatomic gas (H₂) under normal conditions.
- It has **three stable isotopes**: protium (¹H), deuterium (²H), and tritium (³H). Tritium is radioactive and used in nuclear applications.
- **Physically**, it’s a light, colorless, odorless, and highly flammable gas with a very low boiling point.
- **Chemically**, it forms a wide range of compounds, from simple hydrides (e.g., NaH) to complex organometallics. Its high ionization energy and electronegativity make it a strong reducing agent.
- **Astrophysically**, hydrogen fusion powers stars, releasing vast amounts of energy.
- **Technologically**, hydrogen is central to fuel cells, rocket propulsion, and emerging hydrogen‑based energy systems.

Feel free to ask if you’d like deeper details on any specific property or application!
